h1: Planning staff leave around festivals and peak weekends
title: Staff Leave Around Festivals and Peaks | Craft Beer School
desc: How brewpubs can plan staff leave around Indian festivals, New Year and peak weekends without burning out the team or leaving the floor short.
teaser: Everyone wants Diwali off. Your busiest nights are around Diwali. A leave plan settles that in September, not on the day.
standfirst: A brewpub's busiest days are everyone else's holidays. Staff still need rest, family time and festivals at home. A clear leave plan balances both and stops the same people giving up every festival.
sections:
Before you set any leave rules, look at last year's sales by week. Most Indian brewpubs see the same pattern: Friday and Saturday nights, long weekends, the festive season, Christmas to New Year and big sporting events. Local festivals matter too. Brewpubs in Bengaluru, Pune and Kolkata each have different peaks.

Mark these on a 12 month calendar. Rate each week as peak, busy or normal. That calendar is the base for every leave decision you make this year. If you are new and have no sales history, ask neighbouring restaurants or use public holiday lists as a starting point.
Set blackout windows, but keep them few

A blackout window is a period when nobody takes planned leave. Use them sparingly. If every festival is blacked out, staff from other states never get home for their own celebrations and you will lose them. We would black out no more than three or four short windows a year, such as the main festive weekend, Christmas Eve to New Year's Day and your own anniversary event.

Write the windows in the handbook and the appointment letter so new staff know before they join. People accept clear rules much more easily than surprises.
Cap the share of the team away at once

Outside blackout windows, set a simple cap on how many people can be on leave in any week. A common rule is no more than one in four of any team at once. For a bar team of eight, that means two people away at most. For a brewing team of two, it means the brewer and assistant never take leave the same week.

Apply the cap by team, not just overall. Having three kitchen staff off at once is a different problem from having three bartenders off.

The fairest system is a rotation. If someone works Diwali this year, they get first choice of Diwali or another festival next year. Keep a simple record of who worked which festival, so the same people are not always on shift. Staff from different communities and regions will want different festivals off: Eid, Onam, Pongal, Durga Puja, Christmas and others. A diverse team can often cover each other naturally.

Ask for festival leave requests early, at least six to eight weeks ahead. First come first served sounds fair but rewards whoever checks the roster most often. A rotation is better.

Leave planning in the brewhouse works on a longer clock than the bar. An ale takes two to three weeks from brew day to glass. A lager can take four to six weeks. If your brewer is away the week before a festival, the beer for that festival needs to be brewed well before they leave.

Work backwards from each peak. If you expect to sell twice your normal volume over a festive weekend, brew the extra beer three to six weeks earlier, depending on style. Book the brewer's leave for a quieter period afterwards. Our guide to planning a brewing schedule covers the tank side.

When peaks and leave clash, add people rather than burning out the regulars. Trained casual staff, students who worked with you before and cross-trained team members can all help. Bring them in for a paid briefing a week before the peak so they know the beers, the till and the safety rules.

Plan the cash as well. Extra staff, overtime and extra beer all cost money before the peak revenue arrives. If excise payments fall in the same weeks, the squeeze can be sharp. Our guide to planning cash around excise dates shows how to see it coming.

A leave plan only works if staff can see it. Publish rosters at least two weeks ahead, or four weeks ahead during the festive season. Use one shared roster that shows shifts and approved leave together, in a format staff can check on their phones. Make swaps go through the manager so the cap on leave and the cover on each shift stay intact.

Keep a small reserve. On peak nights, roster one more person than you think you need, or keep a trained casual on call. Someone will fall ill on the busiest Saturday of the year. Planning for it costs one extra wage. Not planning for it costs a slow, stressed service in front of your largest crowd of the year.

After a big festival run, staff need recovery time. Plan a quieter roster for the week after, with extra days off for those who worked the peak. Check the weekly off and leave rules for your state, since these vary. Make sure nobody works more days in a row than the rules allow.

A tired team pours slowly, makes mistakes and leaves for jobs with saner hours. Planning leave well is part of the bigger work of building rosters, budgets and staffing around the real shape of the year.

Your first step: mark your peak weeks for the next 12 months on one calendar and share it with the team this week.
faqs: Should brewpubs ban leave during festivals?
Use a few short blackout windows, not a blanket ban. Rotate festival leave so the same people do not always work.
How many staff can be on leave at once?
A common rule is no more than one in four of any team at once, applied team by team.
How early should a brewery plan beer for a festival?
Work back from the peak: about two to three weeks for ales and four to six weeks for lagers, plus any extra volume you expect to sell.
